      <p>The bacterial genus <em>Delftia</em> was established in 1999,
        giving these versatile microbes a name of their own.</p>
      <details>
        <summary>Explore the name</summary>
        <div class="discover-details">
          <p><em>Delftia acidovorans</em> was previously classified as
            <em>Comamonas acidovorans</em>. The new genus was named after
            Delft, the Dutch city associated with its early isolation.</p>

      </details>
      <p class="discover-source">Source: <a href="#discover-ref-genus">Genus description (1999)</a></p>

      <p>The draft genome of <em>D. tsuruhatensis</em> MTQ3 contains
        about 6.27 million DNA base pairs.</p>
      <details>
        <summary>Explore the genome</summary>
        <div class="discover-details">
          <p>MTQ3 was isolated from the tobacco rhizosphere—the soil around roots.
            Its genome helps researchers ask how bacteria interact with plants.
            This is one strain, not a genome size shared by every <em>Delftia</em>.</p>
          <p><a href="dashboard-genome-comparison.html">Compare two published genomes</a></p>

      <div class="discover-stat">2013</div>
      <h3 id="discover-gold">Turning Gold Toxicity into Opportunity</h3>
      <p>Scientists reported how a molecule from <em>D. acidovorans</em>
        helps turn dissolved gold into solid particles.</p>
      <details>
        <summary>Explore gold biomineralization</summary>
        <div class="discover-details">
          <p>Delftibactin protects the bacterium from toxic dissolved gold by
            promoting its precipitation. The gold changes form—it is not created
            from nothing. This laboratory finding is not proof of safe,
            economical recycling of mixed electronic waste at industrial scale.</p>
          <p><a href="research.html">Discover our research projects</a></p>
        </div>
      </details>
      <p class="discover-source">Source: <a href="#discover-ref-gold">Delftibactin study (2013)</a></p>
    </article>

## What is *Delftia acidovorans*? {#about-delftia}

::: {.research-spotlight}
::: {.research-spotlight-text}
*Delftia acidovorans* is a gram-negative, non-fermentative bacterium first identified in Delft, Netherlands, in soil enriched with acetamide. It thrives in habitats containing high concentrations of heavy metals — copper, cobalt, and even **gold** — and produces a nonribosomal peptide that allows it to precipitate gold out of solution, avoiding toxicity.

Today, *Delftia* is found in waste-contaminated soil, water systems, and drains. Beyond its remarkable environmental capabilities, it is studied as an opportunistic pathogen and explored for applications in:

<span class="tag-chip"><span aria-hidden="true">🏅</span> Gold Biomineralization</span>
<span class="tag-chip"><span aria-hidden="true">♻️</span> E-Waste Recycling</span>
<span class="tag-chip"><span aria-hidden="true">🌿</span> Bioremediation</span>
<span class="tag-chip"><span aria-hidden="true">🧬</span> Genomics</span>
<span class="tag-chip"><span aria-hidden="true">🔬</span> Undergraduate Research</span>

<br/><br/>
<a href="references.html" class="btn-hero btn-primary-hero btn-hero--compact">View Publications →</a>
:::

          "Microbial Superheroes" publications.
        </p>
      </div>

      <div class="feature-card">
        <div class="card-icon" aria-hidden="true">🤖</div>
        <h3>Genomics &amp; Automation</h3>
        <p>
          High-throughput sequencing and automation tools help us decode the genome of
          <em>Delftia</em>. BLAST analyses, bioinformatics pipelines, and cloud computing
          accelerate discovery.
        </p>
      </div>

      <div class="feature-card">
        <div class="card-icon" aria-hidden="true">🌐</div>
        <h3>Citizen Science</h3>
        <p>
          Community annotators collaborate via Hypothes.is to mine the scientific literature
          on <em>Delftia</em> as a pathogen, gold-biomineralizing agent, and e-waste recycler.
        </p>
      </div>

    </div>
  </div>
</section>
